P11450:
# The cannabinoid CB2 agonist LY2828360 suppresses neuropathic pain behavior and attenuates morphine tolerance and conditioned place preference in rats

**Authors:** Kelsey G. Guenther; Jonah L. Wirt; Idaira Oliva; Shahin A. Saberi; Jonathon D. Crystal; Andrea G. Hohmann

**Affiliations:** 1Program in Neuroscience, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN | 2Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN | 3Gill Institute for Neuroscience, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN

## Abstract

Cannabinoid CB2 agonists show promise as analgesics because they lack unwanted side effects associated with direct activation of CB1 receptors. CB2 receptor activation suppresses pathological pain in animal models, but the types of pain that best respond to CB2 agonists are incompletely understood. This gap in knowledge may contribute to failures in clinical translation. We previously showed that the G protein-biased CB2 receptor agonist LY2828360 attenuated the maintenance of neuropathic pain behavior in mouse models of inflammatory and neuropathic pain. Whether this finding generalizes to neuropathic pain induced by traumatic nerve injury or occurs in multiple rodent species remains unknown. Here we show that LY2828360 (3 and 10 mg/kg i.p.), administered acutely, reversed paclitaxel-induced mechanical hypersensitivity in male rats. By contrast, LY2828360 (10 mg/kg i.p.), administered acutely, attenuated mechanical hypersensitivity in a spared nerve injury (SNI) rat model, whereas the low dose (3 mg/kg i.p.) was ineffective. In both models, efficacy of LY2828360 was sustained following 10 days of repeated dosing. LY2828360 (3 mg/kg i.p.) also prevented development of tolerance to the opioid analgesic morphine (6 mg/kg i.p.) in rats with SNI when co-administered. LY2828360 (3 mg/kg i.p.) did not produce preference or aversion in the conditioned place preference (CPP) test in rats when administered alone but blocked CPP to morphine (6 mg/kg i.p.). Lastly, LY2828360 (3 mg/kg i.p.) did not alter the acquisition of i.v. morphine self-administration under fixed ratio 1 (FR1) and 3 (FR3) or motivation to work for morphine under a progressive ratio (PR) schedule of reinforcement.

## Abstract

## Introduction

Chronic pain affects an estimated 30% of people worldwide and presents a major healthcare burden (Cohen et al. 2021). Despite its high prevalence, currently available therapies for the treatment of chronic pain are often insufficient given its treatment-resistant nature. Opioids are an effective class of analgesics for the acute treatment of pain, but unwanted side effects such as physical dependence, respiratory depression and tolerance limit their long-term clinical use (Yekkirala et al. 2017; Coluzzi et al. 2022). Recently, targets within the endocannabinoid system have become an area of interest for the treatment of chronic pain (e.g., Lötsch et al. 2018; Finn et al. 2021). Although agonism of the cannabinoid type 1 (CB1) receptor effectively reduces pain symptoms in both pre-clinical models and human pain patients, direct activation of this receptor produces many of the same limitations attributed to currently available pain therapies (e.g., sedation, tolerance, and dependence; Cooper and Haney 2009; Rahn and Hohmann 2009). Instead, activation of the cannabinoid type 2 (CB2) receptor shows a favorable therapeutic profile as it alleviates behavioral hypersensitivities to cutaneous stimulation that are consistent with pathological pain in preclinical studies without producing adverse cannabimimetic effects (Guindon and Hohmann, 2008; Deng et al. 2015; Cabañero et al. 2021). The apparent safety of CB2 receptor activation is often attributed to localization of CB2 receptors primarily to immune cells and low expression in the central nervous system (Galiegue et al. 1995; Howlett et al. 2002; Pacher and Mechoulam 2011).

Despite a promising pre-clinical literature supporting the use of CB2 agonists for the treatment of pain, there has been a failure to translate these results to humans. The generalization of underlying disease conditions across species can lead to loss of translatability from animals in preclinical studies to humans in clinical trials. Consequently, it is imperative to understand which pain types respond best to treatment with CB2 agonists and test for analgesic efficacy in therapeutic conditions in human patients that align with preclinical data. Recently, the CB2 agonist LY2828360 has been investigated for the treatment of pain both pre-clinically and in human pain patients. In mice, LY2828360 showed therapeutic efficacy in preclinical models of neuropathic (Lin et al. 2018; Lin et al. 2022; Carey et al. 2023; Guenther et al. 2024) and inflammatory (Guenther et al. 2023) pain. In humans, LY2828360 was tested in a Phase 2 clinical trial for osteoarthritis pain and failed to meet clinical end points in this sample of patients but was demonstrated to be safe for human consumption (Pereira et al. 2013). Given its apparent safety and similar affinity for human and rat CB2 receptors (Hollinshead et al. 2013), further investigation into the analgesic potential of LY2828360 using preclinical pain models is warranted. This is necessary to fully understand the range of therapeutic benefits of this CB2 agonist and identify which pain states it can best treat.

The opioid and endocannabinoid systems have been shown to functionally interact during the treatment of pain (Bushlin et al. 2022; Wolyniak et al. 2022). CB2 receptor expression is increased following repeated administration of morphine (Zhang et al. 2017) and CB2 receptor activation contributes to the pain alleviating effects of morphine under both normal and inflammatory conditions (Lim et al. 2005; Merighi et al. 2012; Desroches et al. 2014). Furthermore, LY2828350 synergizes with morphine to reduce mechanical hypersensitivity (i.e., as reflected in a lowered threshold for paw withdrawal from mechanical stimulation applied to the plantar paw surface) in paclitaxel-treated mice (Iyer et al. 2020) and prevents and/or reverses tolerance to the analgesic effects of morphine in a variety of neuropathic pain models (Lin et al. 2018; Carey et al. 2023; Guenther et al. 2024). These observations suggest that adjunctive therapies may enhance analgesia and/or produce opioid sparing effects.

The present studies examined the ability of LY2828360 to reduce mechanical hypersensitivity in rat models of traumatic nerve injury and toxic neuropathy, and to determine whether LY2828360 could interfere with the reinforcing effects of morphine in male rats. We previously showed that LY2828360 suppresses mechanical and cold hypersensitivity induced by the chemotherapeutic drug paclitaxel (Lin et al. 2018; Guenther et al. 2024). However, all prior evaluations of the therapeutic efficacy of LY2828360 were performed in mice. Given the heterogeneity of the CB2 receptor across species it is important to evaluate whether the effects seen in mice generalize to other species (Brown et al. 2002). Thus, we asked whether LY2828360 could reduce or prevent mechanical hypersensitivity without the development of tolerance in a rat model of paclitaxel-induced neuropathy (Polomano et al. 2001; Rahn et al. 2008; Deng et al. 2012; Rahn et al. 2014). We also asked whether LY2828360 would be efficacious in a spared nerve injury (SNI) rat model (Decosterd and Woolf 2000), given that this compound has never been examined in any traumatic nerve injury model. LY2828360 prevents the development of morphine tolerance in mouse toxic neuropathy models (Lin et al. 2018; Carey et al. 2023; Guenther et al. 2024). We, therefore, evaluated whether this effect would generalize to a traumatic nerve injury model by co-administering LY2828360 and morphine to rats with SNI across multiple days. Abuse liability is a major limitation of narcotic analgesics. Therefore, it is vital to test new analgesic compounds for potential abuse liability. Thus, we asked whether LY2828360 would produce preference or aversion in a conditioned place preference (CPP) paradigm and whether it could enhance or interfere with morphine-induced place preference in this test in rats. Lastly, we sought to determine whether LY2828360 could alter the reinforcing properties of morphine using an intravenous (i.v.) drug self-administration paradigm. Specifically, we investigated whether LY2828360 would affect the acquisition of i.v. morphine self-administration behavior under fixed ratio 1 (FR1) and 3 (FR3) schedules or alter the motivation to work to obtain morphine infusions using a progressive ratio (PR) schedule of reinforcement in rats.

## Methods

### Subjects

A total of 182 adult male Sprague-Dawley rats (Envigo, Indianapolis, IN) between the age of 90–100 days at the start of experiments were used. Rats were single-housed in a temperature-controlled colony room on a 12/12-hr light/dark cycle (lights off at 8am; lights on at 8pm). All behavioral testing occurred during the dark cycle under red light. Rats were maintained on ad libitum food and water other than during food restriction (15 mg/day) for food lever training. All experiments were approved by the Indiana University Animal Care and Use Committee.

### Drugs

Paclitaxel (Tecoland Corporation, Irvine, CA) was dissolved in a vehicle consisting of 5% cremophor EL (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO), 5% ethanol (Sigma-Aldrich) and 90% saline (0.9%; Aqualite System; Hospira, Inc., Lake Forest, IL) as previously described (Deng et al. 2015). LY2828360 (8-(2-chlorophenyl)-2-methyl-6-(4-methylpiperazin-1- yl)-9-(tetrahydro-2H-pyran-4-yl)-9H- purine) was synthesized by Sai Biotech (Mumbai, India; purity >98%). AM630 was a gift from Alexandros Makriyannis (Northeastern University, Boston, MA). Morphine sulfate was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. LY2828360, morphine and AM630 were dissolved in vehicle containing 3% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO; Sigma-Aldrich), 5% emulphor (Alkamuls EL-620; Rhodia, Cranbury, NJ), 5% ethanol and 87% saline for intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection. For i.v. self-administration, morphine was dissolved in saline. Paclitaxel and AM630 were administered in a volume of 1 ml/kg i.p. LY2828360 was administered in a volume of 2 ml/kg i.p. to account for the limited solubility of this compound. Morphine was similarly administered in a volume of 2 ml/kg i.p. for von Frey experiments to match LY2828360 injection volumes, 1 ml/kg i.p. for conditioned place preference (CPP) experiments and at 100 ug/kg/infusion for intravenous (i.v.) self-administration.

### Paclitaxel-induced neuropathy

Paclitaxel (2 mg/kg i.p.) was administered four times on alternate days (cumulative dose of 8 mg/kg) to rats to model the clinical phenomenon of chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy as previously described (Polomano et al. 2001; Rahn et al. 2011). Control rats received an equal volume of cremophor-based vehicle. The presence of paclitaxel-induced mechanical hypersensitivity was verified by measuring paw withdrawal thresholds prior to pharmacological manipulation 14 days after initial paclitaxel injection in all experiments apart from the study employing prophylactic dosing.

### Spared nerve injury surgery

SNI surgery was performed unilaterally in rats to model the clinical phenomenon of traumatic nerve injury-induced neuropathy as described previously (Decosterd and Woolf 2000; Gutierrez et al. 2011; Gutierrez et al. 2021). Briefly, rats were deeply anesthetized with isoflurane, the flank of the rat was shaved and prepared for aseptic surgery. Then, a small incision (approximately 1.5 cm) was made on the flank of the rat and the underlying biceps femoris muscle was gently separated to expose the sciatic nerve. The common peroneal and tibial branches of the sciatic nerve were tightly ligated with a silk suture (5–0 PERMA-HAND Silk Suture, Ethicon) then cut, leaving the sural branch intact. The muscle was then closed and held together with a single silk suture before closing the skin incision with nylon sutures (4–0 ETHILON Black Monofilament, Ethicon), which were removed 1-week post-surgery. Rats were not tested in the initial 2-week period following SNI surgery to allow them to recover from both the surgery and the acute inflammatory phase of SNI. SNI produces behavioral hypersensitivity to mechanical stimulation of the paw ipsilateral to the injury. The presence of SNI-induced mechanical hypersensitivity was verified by measuring paw withdrawal thresholds prior to pharmacological manipulation in all experiments.

### Jugular catheter surgery

Backmount catheters were implanted into the left jugular vein of rats as described previously (Gutierrez et al. 2011; Gutierrez et al. 2021; Oliva et al. 2022). Briefly, rats were deeply anesthetized with isoflurane and the neck and area behind the shoulder blades were shaved and prepared for aseptic surgery. Two incisions were made, one slightly below and between the shoulder blades on the dorsal surface of the rat (approximately 2 cm) and on the neck above the location of the jugular vein (approximately 1.5 cm). The silastic tubing of the catheter was passed subcutaneously from the back incision to the neck incision. The jugular vein was then isolated from surrounding tissue and a small hole was made in the vein with a 25G needle. The catheter tubing was inserted approximately 3.5 cm into the jugular vein and secured with silk sutures. Nylon sutures were used to close the skin incisions and were removed 2-weeks post-surgery.

### General in vivo experimental procedures

In all studies, the experimenter was blinded to pharmacological manipulations.

#### Mechanical paw withdrawal threshold measurement

Paw withdrawal thresholds were measured using an electronic von Frey anesthesiometer (IITC model Alemo 2290–4, Woodland Hills, CA) as described in our previously published work (Rahn et al. 2008; Deng et al. 2012; Rahn et al. 2014; Gutierrez et al. 2011; Gutierrez et al. 2021). Rats were placed on a testing table with a stainless-steel wire mesh flooring (1.2 × 1.2 cm gaps in wire mesh) and confined under a clear Plexiglas chamber (13.5 × 13.5 × 23.5 cm) for at least 30 minutes before testing. Following habituation, a mechanical force was applied to the hind paw until a paw withdrawal response was observed. In the paclitaxel experiments, force was applied to the midplantar region of the hind paw, whereas in the spared nerve injury (SNI) experiments force was applied closer to the lateral edge of the paw to stimulate the site of injury of this model (Cichon et al. 2018). Each paw was measured twice at each time point in a right-left-right-left order with an interstimulation interval of several minutes between paws. Specifically, the right paw was tested for all rats before moving on to test the left paw for all rats and so on for each time point; testing the entire right-left-right left sequence for any given rat took approximately 15 minutes. All four measurements of mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds were averaged in rats that received toxic challenge with paclitaxel. Paw withdrawal thresholds (measured in duplicate) were averaged separately for the paw ipsilateral and contralateral to SNI.

#### Experiment 1: Impact of LY2828360 in the paclitaxel model

First, we examined the duration of action of LY2828360, administered acutely, in suppressing mechanical hypersensitivity in rats with established paclitaxel-induced neuropathy. Baseline mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds were measured, then rats received a single injection of LY2828360 (3 or 10 mg/kg i.p.) or vehicle (i.p.), and mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds were measured again at 0.5, 2, 4 and 6 hours post-injection (n = 6 per group).

In a separate cohort of rats, we examined the ability of AM630 to prevent LY2828360 from increasing mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds in rats with established paclitaxel-induced neuropathy. Baseline mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds were measured, then rats were pretreated with AM630 (3 mg/kg i.p.) 20 minutes prior to either LY2828360 (3 mg/kg i.p.) or vehicle (i.p.). The control group in this study received vehicle (i.p.) 20 minutes prior to a subsequent injection of vehicle (i.p.) to ensure that injection volumes were matched in all conditions. Mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds were measured again at 0.5, 2, 4 and 6 hours post-injection (i.e., the same post-injection timepoints measured in the acute dosing study) (n = 6 per group).

We also examined the efficacy of chronic LY2828360 in rats with established paclitaxel-induced neuropathy using the same rats that received these pharmacological treatments in the acute study. LY2828360 (3 mg/kg i.p.) or vehicle (i.p.) was administered once daily for 10 consecutive days. Mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds were measured on day 1, 4, 7 and 10 of chronic dosing, both 30 minutes post-injection and immediately prior to injections (i.e., as a pre-injection baseline on day 1 and 24 hours following the previous injection of LY2828360/vehicle on subsequent test days). Injections were administered (i.p.) immediately following pre-injection baseline measurements. Mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds were also measured over an additional 10 days following termination of chronic dosing (i.e., on day 11, 14, 17 and 20) to determine whether the therapeutic efficacy of LY2828360 outlasted the duration of chronic dosing. The time point associated with maximal increases in paw withdrawal thresholds in the acute study was used to assess drug efficacy in the chronic dosing study (i.e., 30 minutes post-injection). Day 1 mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds are the same in both acute and chronic dosing components of Experiment 1 (which used the same rats) (n = 6 per group).

We also examined the ability of prophylactic LY2828360 treatment to prevent the development of paclitaxel-induced mechanical hypersensitivity. Rats received once daily injections of either LY2828360 (3 mg/kg i.p. per day) or vehicle (i.p.) for 11 consecutive days during the paclitaxel dosing schedule. Specifically, LY2828360 or vehicle was injected (i.p.) once daily on days 0–10, beginning 24 h prior to initial dosing with paclitaxel or cremophor-based vehicle. Paclitaxel (2 mg/kg i.p.) was injected on days 1, 3, 5 and 7 as described above. On days when both drugs were administered, LY2828360 was injected 30-minutes prior to paclitaxel. Mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds were measured on day 1, 4, 7 and 10 of chronic injections, both prior to injection (pre-injection) and at 30-minutes post-injection. Mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds were also measured over an additional 10 days following termination of chronic dosing (i.e., on day 11, 14, 17 and 20) to examine whether prophylactic treatment with LY2828360 prevented the development of mechanical hypersensitivity after termination of the treatment (n = 6 per group).

#### Experiment 2: Impact of LY2828360 in the SNI model

Experimental procedures were similar to those performed Experiment 1. First, we examined the duration of action of LY2828360, administered acutely, in suppressing mechanical hypersensitivity in rats with established SNI-induced neuropathy. Baseline mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds were measured, then rats received a single injection of LY2828360 (3 or 10 mg/kg i.p.) or vehicle (i.p.), and mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds were measured again at 0.5, 1, 2, 4 and 6 hours post-injection (n = 6 per group).

In a separate cohort of rats, we examined the ability of AM630 to prevent LY2828360 from increasing mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds in rats with established SNI-induced neuropathy. Baseline mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds were measured, then rats were pretreated with AM630 (3 mg/kg i.p.) 20 minutes prior to either LY2828360 (10 mg/kg i.p.) or vehicle (i.p.). The control group in this study received vehicle (i.p.) 20 minutes prior to a subsequent injection of vehicle (i.p.) to ensure injection volumes were matched in all conditions. Mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds were measured again at 0.5, 1, 2, 4 and 6 hours following all injections (i.e., the same post-injection timepoints measured in the acute dosing study) (n = 6 per group).

We also examined the efficacy of chronic LY2828360 in suppressing mechanical hypersensitivity in rats with established SNI-induced neuropathy using the same rats that received these pharmacological treatments in the acute study. LY2828360 (3 or 10 mg/kg i.p.) or vehicle (i.p.) was administered once daily for 10 consecutive days. Mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds were measured on day 1, 4, 7 and 10 of chronic dosing, both 1-hour post-injection and immediately prior to injections (pre-injection). Injections were administered (i.p.) immediately following pre-injection baseline measurements. Mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds were also measured over an additional 7 days following termination of chronic dosing (i.e., on day 11, 14 and 17) to determine whether the therapeutic efficacy of LY2828360 outlasted the duration of chronic dosing. The time point associated with maximal increases in mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds in the acute study was used to assess drug efficacy in the chronic dosing study (i.e., 1-hour post-injection). Day 1 mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds are the same in both acute and chronic dosing components of Experiment 2, (which used the same rats) (n = 6 per group).

#### Experiment 3: Impact of LY2828360 on the development of morphine tolerance

Experimental procedures were conducted identically to those described in Experiment 2. We asked whether the low dose of LY2828360 (3 mg/kg i.p.) would alter the ability of morphine to increase mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds when co-administered acutely in rats with established SNI-induced neuropathy. Baseline mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds were measured, then rats received a single injection of morphine (6 mg/kg i.p.), LY2828360 (3 mg/kg i.p.) co-administered with morphine (6 mg/kg i.p.), or vehicle (i.p.), and mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds were measured again at 0.5, 1, 2, 4 and 6 hours post-injection (n = 7–8 per group).

We also examined the ability of LY2828360 to prevent the development of morphine tolerance in a chronic dosing paradigm in rats with SNI-induced neuropathy using the same rats that received these pharmacological treatments in the acute study. Morphine (6 mg/kg i.p.), LY2828360 (3 mg/kg i.p.) co-administered with morphine (6 mg/kg i.p.), or vehicle (i.p.) was administered once daily for 10 consecutive days. Mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds were measured on day 1, 4, 7 and 10 of chronic dosing, both 1-hour post-injection and immediately prior to injections, and were also measured over an additional 7 days following termination of chronic dosing (i.e., on day 11, 14 and 17). Day 1 mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds are consequently the same in both acute and chronic dosing components of Experiment 3 (which used the same rats) (n = 7–8 per group).

#### Experiment 4: Impact of LY2828360 on morphine-induced conditioned place preference (CPP)

We evaluated whether LY2882360 would produce preference or aversion on its own or alter CPP to morphine in otherwise naïve rats. Methods were similar to those described previously by our group using mice (Slivicki et al. 2020; Iyer et al. 2020). The custom-configured apparatus used in the CPP experiment consisted of 3 chambers separated by mechanical doors; a central neutral (gray) chamber (12 × 21 × 21 cm) was connected on either side to one of two conditioning chambers (21 × 21 × 28 cm). Each conditioning chamber had distinct visual cues (thick vertical or thin horizontal black and white stripes with an equivalent amount of black/white in both chambers) (Med-Associates Inc., St. Albans, VT, USA). The time spent in each chamber was recorded over a 30-minute interval each day. Four different conditioning treatments were tested using the following chamber pairings: (1) one chamber paired with morphine (6 mg/kg i.p.) and the opposite chamber paired with vehicle; (2) both chambers paired with vehicle; (3) one chamber paired with LY2828360 (3 mg/kg i.p.) and the opposite chamber paired with vehicle; and (4) one chamber paired with LY2828360 (3 mg/kg i.p.) followed 30-minutes later by morphine (6 mg/kg i.p.) and the opposite chamber paired with vehicle (n = 6–11 per group). The following protocol was used to test all groups: on days 1 and 2, rats were placed in the middle chamber and allowed to freely roam between all three chambers to habituate to the apparatus. On day 3, rats were again allowed to freely roam the three chambers after which baseline preference assessment was conducted to confirm that rats did not show a bias for either chamber prior to drug pairing. Rats that spent more than 1140 seconds (i.e. 80%) or less than 360 seconds (i.e. 20%) of the baseline trial in either chamber were excluded from the study and never received pharmacological manipulations. The remaining rats were randomly assigned to receive active treatments in the left or right chamber. Next, rats underwent eight days of conditioning trials during which they received an injection of either drug (or vehicle) and then were immediately restricted to a single chamber of the CPP apparatus for 30 minutes. On days 4, 6, 8 and 10 rats received either morphine, vehicle, LY2828360 or LY2882360 followed by morphine and were immediately confined to the drug-paired chamber. On days 5, 7, 9 and 11 rats received an injection of vehicle before being placed in the chamber opposite to the drug-paired chamber. On day 12, rats were placed in the middle chamber and allowed to freely roam between all three chambers to assess the impact of treatment on CPP in a drug-free state.

#### Experiment 5: Impact of LY2828360 on intravenous morphine self-administration

We evaluated whether LY2828360 (3 mg/kg i.p.) would alter the reinforcing effects of morphine using an i.v. self-administration approach in otherwise naïve rats. Methods were similar to those described previously by our group (Gutierrez et al. 2011; Gutierrez et al. 2021; Oliva et al. 2022). Prior to catheter surgery, rats were food restricted (15 mg/day) and trained to lever press for food in an operant chamber (Med-Associates Inc., St. Albans, VT, USA). On day 1 rats underwent a single magazine training session where a food pellet was dispensed every 60 seconds for a total of 30 minutes, with both levers retracted for the entire session. On days 2–5 rats were trained to lever press for food (fixed ratio 1:FR1) on both levers. Specifically, every lever press resulted in one food pellet being dispensed with the extended or retracted lever alternating between the two levers every 10 responses. The session ended after the rat performed 60 lever presses or after 60 minutes elapsed. Rats were returned to ad libitum food prior to jugular catheter surgery. After surgical recovery, rats were food restricted again and re-trained for two sessions of lever training for food. All rats were returned to ad libitum food for the duration of the self-administration experiments. The operant chambers used for self-administration were located in a separate room from those used for food lever training (Med-Associates Inc., St. Albans, VT, USA). Operant chambers were equipped with two retractable levers. Left and right levers were randomly assigned as active or inactive conditions for each rat prior to the start of the experiment. Rats were tested once daily in a 50-minute session during which both levers were extended; responses on the inactive lever resulted in no infusion whereas completing the required number of responses on the active lever resulted in the delivery of a morphine infusion paired with a light cue turning on (i.e. discrete cue) for approximately 6 seconds, followed by a 5 second timeout period. Both levers were retracted for the duration of the infusion and the timeout period. Each morphine infusion delivered approximately 6–8 μl based on the rat’s body weight for a dose of 100 μg/kg/infusion.

In the acquisition experiment, rats were allowed to self-administer morphine for 20 consecutive days: 10 days on FR1 and 10 days on FR3 (n = 6–7 per group). This operant schedule was used to ensure that rats learned to distinguish between the active and inactive lever. Rats received vehicle or LY2828360 (3 mg/kg i.p.) 30 minutes prior to each of the 20 acquisition sessions.

In the progressive ratio (PR) experiment, a new cohort of rats was first allowed to self-administer morphine for 15 days: 5 days on FR1, 5 days on FR3 and 5 days on FR5 (n = 10 per group). Following FR training rats were moved to a progressive ratio (PR) schedule of reinforcement that involved increasing effort within the same session to get an i.v. infusion (i.e. PR values were 1, 2, 4, 9, 12, 15, 20, 25, 32, 40, 50, 62, 77, 95, 118, 145, 178, 219, 268, 328, 402, 492, 603, 737, 901, 1102, 1347, 1647, 2012). Once rats reached stable lever pressing behavior in PR, defined as less than 15% variance in the number of infusions for three consecutive days (Oliva et al. 2021), they were given LY2828360 (3 mg/kg i.p.) 30 minutes prior to morphine PR self-administration for 5 consecutive days. The number of active and inactive lever presses as well as the number of infusions and the last ratio completed was recorded for each rat.

### Statistical analysis

Paw withdrawal thresholds were averaged across duplicate determinations separately for ipsilateral and contralateral paws in SNI studies and across both paws in paclitaxel studies for each subject. Mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds, CPP data and data derived from i.v. self-administration studies employing the FR schedule were analyzed by Two-way repeated measures ANOVA. Tukey’s multiple comparisons post hoc tests were subsequently used to determine which conditions differed from each other for experiments employing more than two groups. Sidak’s multiple comparisons post hoc test was used for two group comparisons. Two-tailed unpaired t-tests were used to determine significant differences between two groups in the self-administration studies employing the PR schedule. All statistical analyses were performed using Graphpad Prism 7 using the post hoc tests recommended by the program (Graphpad Prism software, San Diego, CA).

## Results

### Experiment 1: Impact of LY2828360 in the paclitaxel model

Paclitaxel treatment reduced mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds prior to pharmacological manipulations in all Experiment 1 studies (p < 0.0001) (see Supplemental Table 1). In paclitaxel-treated rats, LY2828360 (3–10 mg/kg i.p.) treatment increased mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds relative to vehicle, paw withdrawal thresholds changed across time and the interaction was significant (Group: F2,15 = 23.95, p < 0.0001; Time: F3,45 = 11.92, p < 0.0001; Interaction: F6,45 = 4.704, p = 0.0009) (Fig. 1A). Both the low (3 mg/kg i.p.) and high (10 mg/kg i.p.) doses of LY2828360, which showed similar efficacy overall, increased mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds relative to vehicle across the observation interval (p < 0.0008 for each comparison; Tukey’s multiple comparison test). Tukey’s multiple comparison post hoc tests also revealed that LY2828360 (3 mg/kg i.p.) increased mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds 0.5 (p < 0.0001), 2 (p < 0.0001) and 4 h (p = 0.0006) post-injection whereas LY2828360 (10 mg/kg i.p.) increased paw withdrawal thresholds at 2 (p < 0.0001) and 4 h (p = 0.0037) post-injection relative to vehicle (Fig. 1A).

In the AM630 blockade study, mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds differed as a function of drug treatment in paclitaxel-treated rats overall, but did not differ as a function of time, and the interaction between drug treatment and time was not significant (Group: F2,15 = 3.82, p = 0.0456; Time: F3,45 = 1.22, p = 0.3134; Interaction: F6,45 = 1.884, p = 0.1044) (Fig. 1B). However, Tukey’s multiple comparison post hoc test failed to reveal significant differences between groups; mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds in the group co-administered LY2828360 (3 mg/kg i.p.) and AM630 (3 mg/kg i.p.) only trended higher than those treated with vehicle (p = 0.058) (Fig. 1B).

In paclitaxel-treated rats, chronic dosing with LY2828360 increased post-injection mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds relative to vehicle treatment, paw withdrawal thresholds changed across time and the interaction was significant (Group: F2,15 = 333, p < 0.0001; Time: F3,45 = 6.668, p = 0.0008; Interaction: F6,45 = 3.006, p = 0.0148) (Fig. 2A). LY2828360 (3 mg/kg i.p.) increased paw withdrawal thresholds across the chronic dosing interval relative to vehicle in paclitaxel-treated rats (p < 0.0001; Tukey’s multiple comparison test) and also differed from the Cremophor vehicle-treated control group (p = 0.0261; Tukey’s multiple comparison test). Tukey’s multiple comparison post hoc test also revealed that LY2828360 (3 mg/kg i.p.) increased mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds relative to vehicle on day 1, 4, 7 and 10 of repeated injections (p < 0.0001 for all time-points). No difference in mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds were observed between day 1 and day 10 of LY2828360 injections (3 mg/kg i.p.), consistent with the absence of tolerance (p =0.0900) (Fig. 2A). Chronic administration of LY2828360 also increased pre-injection (i.e., testing that occurred 24-hrs after the previous injection) mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds relative to vehicle treatment overall and the interaction was significant (Group: F2,15 = 100.2, p < 0.0001; Time: F3,45 = 2.493, p = 0.0721; Interaction: F6,45 = 5.471, p = 0.0003) (Fig. 2B). LY2828360 (3 mg/kg i.p.) increased mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds relative to vehicle across the observation interval, but also differed from the cremophor-vehicle treated group (p < 0.0001 for each comparison; Tukey’s multiple comparison test), suggesting that this dose did not fully reverse mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds to control levels. ## Discussion

Here we show that the CB2 agonist LY2828360 suppresses mechanical hypersensitivity in mechanistically distinct models of neuropathic pain in male rats. Our results are the first to demonstrate that LY2828360 reduces mechanical hypersensitivity in a traumatic nerve injury model (SNI). We are also the first to show that LY2828360 reduces paclitaxel-evoked mechanical hypersensitivity and suppresses tolerance to morphine in paclitaxel-treated rats. LY2828360, administered acutely, reduced mechanical hypersensitivity at lower doses in the paclitaxel-induced neuropathy model than in the SNI model, suggesting that LY2828360 may be less potent in reversing mechanical hypersensitivity caused by traumatic nerve injury compared to paclitaxel treatment. We have also shown that higher doses of LY2828360 are necessary to reduce mechanical hypersensitivity induced by the inflammatory agent carrageenan compared to toxic neuropathy induced by either paclitaxel or ddC treatment in mice (Carey et al. 2023; Guenther et al. 2023; Guenther et al. 2024). Potency of LY2828360 in suppressing mechanical hypersensitivity may be dependent on the pain model evaluated, suggesting the need to align efficacy of CB2 receptor agonist treatment with the appropriate therapeutic indication. These observations have clinical relevance given that LY2828360 failed in a clinical trial of osteoarthritis pain (Pereira et al. 2013). In our studies, putative anti-nociceptive effects of LY2828360 were mediated by the CB2 receptor as they were blocked by the CB2 receptor antagonist AM630. We previously showed that the effects of LY2828360 in the paclitaxel model are mediated by the CB2 receptor in mice and used a conditional knockout mouse model to show that these effects are specifically dependent upon CB2 receptors in primary sensory neurons (Lin et al. 2018; Guenther et al. 2024).

One major limitation of current pain treatment such as narcotic analgesics is the development of tolerance (e.g., Rosenblum et al. 2008; Gurtskaia et al. 2014). Here we show that LY2828360 retains its putative analgesic properties after 10 days of repeated administration in both paclitaxel- and SNI-induced neuropathy models. LY2828360 also exhibited sustained therapeutic efficacy when administered chronically in mice with paclitaxel- (Lin et al. 2018; Guenther et al. 2024) or ddC-induced neuropathy (Carey et al. 2023). Interestingly, the low dose of LY2828360 (3 mg/kg i.p.), which did not enhance effects of morphine when administered acutely in the SNI model, increased mechanical withdrawal thresholds after several days of repeated administration. A carry-over effect of chronic LY2828360 administration was also observed. Rats exhibited a sustained increase in mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds measured 24 hours after the previous injection of LY2828360 in both neuropathic pain models. After the termination of repeated dosing with LY2828360, mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds subsequently returned to pre-treatment baseline levels. Thus, LY2828360 did not permanently prevent neuropathy. Additional pharmacokinetic studies are required to ascertain levels of LY2828360 in brain and plasma in rats with SNI at multiple timepoints following acute and chronic dosing. Our results are consistent with the literature which shows CB2 receptor agonists retaining their efficacy in suppressing behavioral hypersensitivities to mechanical and cold stimulation following repeated administration (eg. Romero-Sandoval et al. 2008; Deng et al. 2015; Niu et al. 2017; Mlost et al. 2021).

Given the difficulties of treating chronic neuropathic pain, efforts to prevent the development of these conditions are needed. We examined the ability of prophylactic administration of LY2828360 to prevent paclitaxel-induced neuropathy and found that LY28282360 delayed the development of mechanical hypersensitivity in this model but did not permanently prevent it. Specifically, LY2828360 increased mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds during the development phase when drug was being administered, but mechanical hypersensitivity emerged once LY2828360 administration was no longer administered. A similar result was previously reported using a mouse model of paclitaxel-induced neuropathy (Guenther et al. 2024).

Opioids are often prescribed for pain management but tolerance to their anti-nociceptive effects often leads to overuse and abuse. Consequently, recent interest in the treatment of pain has incorporated co-administration of opioids with mechanistically distinct analgesic compounds to prevent the development of opioid tolerance (eg. Habibi-Asl et al. 2014; Mansouri et al. 2015; Hassanipour et al. 2016; Hosseinzadeh et al. 2016). In the present study, the low dose LY2828360 prevented the development of morphine tolerance in a traumatic nerve injury model at a dose that did not alter the acute effect of morphine. These results support previous findings from our lab that show LY2828360 similarly preventing the development of morphine tolerance in the paclitaxel (Lin et al. 2018; Guenther et al. 2024) and ddC (Carey et al. 2023) neuropathy models in mice. CB2 agonists can synergize with morphine to reduce pain behavior (Grenald et al. 2017; Iyer et al. 2020) and have also been shown to reduce morphine tolerance in a rat model of cancer pain (Zhang et al. 2016; Zhang et al. 2017) and a mouse model of inflammatory pain (Yuill et al. 2017), but the mechanism for this effect is not yet known. The activation of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) resulting in microglial activation and the release of inflammatory factors such as IL-1β, IL-6 and TNF-α is necessary for the development of morphine tolerance (Kong et al. 2022; Cui et al. 2023). CB2 receptor activation has been shown to reduce phosphorylation of the p38 MAPK pathway (Paszcuk et al. 2011), the ERK1/2 pathway (Merighi et al. 2012) and the JNK pathway (Yuill et al. 2017) and suppresses the inflammatory response of microglial cells (Romero-Sandoval et al. 2008) to reduce morphine tolerance. Interestingly, CB2 receptors on CX3CR1-expressing microglia/macrophages do not seem to play a role in preventing morphine tolerance in a mouse model of chemotherapy-induced neuropathy based upon our studies employing conditional deletion of CB2 from CX3CR1-expressing microglia/macrophages (Guenther et al. 2024). Instead, activation of CB2 receptors on peripheral sensory neurons appears to play an integral role in preventing or reversing morphine tolerance in this model (Guenther et al. 2024), as these effects were absent in mice with a conditional deletion of CB2 from peripheral sensory neurons.

Another major limitation of narcotic analgesics is their potential for misuse and abuse. We found that LY2828360 does not produce preference or aversion in a CPP test. Furthermore, LY2828360 prevented the development of CPP to morphine in rats, establishing generalizability of previous findings in mice. Our results align with previous studies by our group and others showing that CB2 receptor activation blocks morphine-induced place preference in the CPP test in mice (Grenald et al. 2017; Iyer et al. 2020). Furthermore, a low dose of LY2828360 (3 mg/kg i.p.) did not impede or enhance either the acquisition of intravenous morphine self-administration. Likewise, LY2828360 (3 mg/kg i.p.) did not alter the motivation to work for morphine infusions, suggesting that the actions of CB2 receptor agonist may differ when measuring conditioned drug-context association (non-contingent i.p. morphine administration) versus conditioned reinforcement (contingent i.v. morphine self-administration). CB2 receptor activation has also been shown to reduce cocaine (Xi et al. 2011) and ethanol (Mansouri et al. 2014) self-administration in mice. However, to our knowledge, our work is the first to examine the effects of CB2 receptor agonism on opioid self-administration. CB2 receptors have been a target of interest for regulating drug dependence since their discovery in brain regions involved in reward, including the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and the nucleus accumbens (NAcc; García-Gutiérrez et al. 2010; Navarrete et al. 2021). CB2 receptor activation in these reward related regions has been reported to reduce the firing of dopamine neurons in the VTA (Zhang et al. 2015; Zhang et al. 2017) and attenuate increases in dopamine caused by rewarding drugs in the NAcc (Xi et al. 2011). LY2828360 has also been shown to attenuate fentanyl-induced respiratory depression in mice further supporting evidence of CB2-opioid interactions (Zavala et al. 2020), but whether this effect is observed in rats remains unknown. More work is needed to determine the mechanism through which LY2828360 reduces place preference caused by morphine in rats.

One limitation of the current work is that female rats were not tested. Previous work using mice shows that LY2828360 is similarly efficacious in preclinical pain models induced by paclitaxel, ddC or carrageenan in mice of both sexes (Carey et al. 2023; Guenther et al. 2023; Guenther et al. 2024). However, CB2 receptor mediated prevention of morphine tolerance appears to be sex dependent with little or no efficacy seen in female mice in any pain models tested to date (Carey et al. 2023; Guenther et al. 2024). Hence, we focused our initial studies evaluating impact of LY2828360 on the reinforcing properties of morphine on male rats. Further work is needed to determine the efficacy of LY2828360 in both the paclitaxel and SNI models in female rats and to elucidate the complex role of CB2 receptors in the development of morphine tolerance and the role of sex in this phenomenon. Similarly, more work is needed to determine whether LY2828360 can prevent morphine-induced place preference or whether it interferes with i.v. morphine self-administration in female rats.

LY2828360 is a G protein-biased CB2 receptor agonist that exhibits slow signaling through adenylyl cyclase (Lin et al. 2018), penetrates the central nervous system and has similar affinity for human and rat CB2 receptors (Hollinshead et al. 2013). Given the prevalence of ligand-dependent biased signaling exhibited by the CB2 receptor (e.g. Atwood et al. 2012; Soethoudt et al. 2017), it is important to consider the signaling profile of CB2 agonists when examining their effects in various preclinical models. We did not evaluate whether signaling bias is necessary or dispensable for the pattern of effects observed herein or whether the same pattern of results would be obtained with CB2 agonists exhibiting a more balanced signaling profile. Overall, LY2828360 may be a useful first-line treatment for human pain patients, not only due to its ability to supress pain behavior with sustained efficacy, but also because it prevents the development of opioid tolerance in a variety of pain types and potentially interferes with morphine-induced drug context association. However, LY2828360 did not enhance or impede the reinforcing effects of morphine under our testing conditions in our i.v. self-administration studies. Although LY2828360 failed for efficacy in a phase 2 clinical trial in osteoarthritis pain, a growing body of evidence suggests that it should be reconsidered for clinical application in neuropathic pain conditions.

## Abstract

Hidradenoma is an uncommon benign neoplasm of sweat gland origin, and its malignant counterpart, hidradenocarcinoma, presents with similar morphology and histology and can behave aggressively with metastasis and recurrence. These adnexal tumors represent a diagnostic challenge, and to provide a more robust clinical context of hidradenoma and hidradenocarcinoma, we performed a natural-language query for corresponding medical records from January 2000 through April 2023 in our center. 64 cases met the criteria for analysis with diagnoses of hidradenoma (n = 39), hidradenocarcinoma (n = 20), or malignant transformation from hidradenoma to hidradenocarcinoma (n = 5). Information on patient demographics, tumor location, treatment modalities, and disease outcomes were collected. Overall, this review highlights the real-life clinical context of hidradenoma/hidradenocarcinoma in a medical center. Tumors were identified on every major body surface; wide local excision is the standard of care, while chemotherapy and radiation were used sparingly, and recurrence, malignant transformation, and diseaseassociated morbidity are rare.

## Main Text

Hidradenoma is an uncommon benign neoplasm of sweat gland origin that usually presents as a solitary, well-circumscribed, skin-colored or erythematous nodule [4]. Its malignant counterpart, hidradenocarcinoma, arises de-novo or from untreated hidradenoma and can behave aggressively with metastasis and recurrence [5]. These adnexal tumors present diagnostic challenges because of their overlapping features with one another and other cutaneous neoplasms and their frequent deviation from classic histopathologic morphologies [3]. Their histopathologic variability is underscored by the multiple terms used to describe hidradenoma and hidradenocarcinoma [5]. Diagnostic uncertainty can lead to misclassification of disease with consequent clinical impact [1]. To provide a more robust clinical context that can assist with the diagnosis and understanding of these neoplasms, we describe demographic and clinical characteristics for 64 patients diagnosed with hidradenoma and hidradenocarcinoma.

We performed a natural-language query for medical records from Massachusetts General Hospital and Brigham and Women’s Hospital to identify all patients from January 2000 through April 2023 with biopsy-proven diagnoses of hidradenoma, hidradenocarcinoma, or malignant transformation from hidradenoma to hidradenocarcinoma. A total of 64 cases met the criteria for analysis with diagnoses of hidradenoma (n=39), hidradenocarcinoma (n=20), or malignant transformation from hidradenoma to hidradenocarcinoma (n=5) (Table 1 and Table 2). Of these patients, 35 (54.7%) were males and 29 (45.3%) were females; 54 (84.4%) were white/Caucasian. Tumors were diagnosed on every major body surface, with the face (n=10, 15.6%) and scalp (n=7, 10.9%) being the most common sites. 44 (68.8%) patients underwent wide local excision of their tumor, 5 (7.8%) received radiotherapy, and 1 (1.6%) patient received chemotherapy. Malignant transformation from hidradenoma to hidradenocarcinoma resulted from untreated hidradenoma (n=2) and inadequate benign tumor excision

Several findings in our study contribute to the existing knowledge and understanding of hidradenoma and its malignant counterpart. Our analysis demonstrated a similar distribution between the sexes for hidradenoma (18 females, 21 males), though in the 25 malignant cases, males were overrepresented (n=17, 68%) compared to females (n=8, 32%). The low utilization of chemotherapy and radiotherapy suggests these modalities are typically reserved for potentially more aggressive initial presentations. Our study also highlights the rarity of disease-associated morbidity, recurrence, and distant metastasis, consistent with other findings of hidradenocarcinoma in the literature [2]. Nevertheless, the identification of distant metastasis in a subset of hidradenocarcinoma cases emphasizes the importance of vigilant monitoring and early intervention in high-risk patients. Additionally, the association of malignant transformation with untreated hidradenoma and inadequate benign tumor excision reiterates the critical role of timely and appropriate interventions.

Our findings are limited by the retrospective nature of the analysis over a single multicenter setting. The observed clinical patterns, treatment approaches, and outcomes may aid clinicians in the diagnosis and management of these rare sweat gland neoplasms. Further research is warranted to validate our findings and enhance the current understanding of the clinical spectrum of hidradenoma and hidradenocarcinoma, especially regarding factors that potentially influence malignancy risk such as tumor site and patient sex.

# Inhibition of PSD95‐nNOS protein–protein interactions decreases morphine reward and relapse vulnerability in rats

**Authors:** Idaira Oliva; Shahin A Saberi; Claudia Rangel‐Barajas; Vishakh Iyer; Kendra D Bunner; Yvonne Y Lai; Pushkar M Kulkarni; Sumanta Garai; Ganesh A Thakur; Jonathon D Crystal; George V Rebec; Andrea G Hohmann

**Affiliations:** 1 Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA | 2 Program in Neuroscience, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA | 3 Department of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Northeastern University, Boston, MA, USA | 4 Gill Center for Biomolecular Science, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA

## Abstract

Glutamate signalling through the N‐methyl‐d‐aspartate receptor (NMDAR) activates the enzyme neuronal nitric oxide synthase (nNOS) to produce the signalling molecule nitric oxide (NO). We hypothesized that disruption of the protein–protein interaction between nNOS and the scaffolding protein postsynaptic density 95 kDa (PSD95) would block NMDAR‐dependent NO signalling and represent a viable therapeutic route to decrease opioid reward and relapse‐like behaviour without the unwanted side effects of NMDAR antagonists. We used a conditioned place preference (CPP) paradigm to evaluate the impact of two small‐molecule PSD95‐nNOS inhibitors, IC87201 and ZL006, on the rewarding effects of morphine. Both IC87201 and ZL006 blocked morphine‐induced CPP at doses that lacked intrinsic rewarding or aversive properties. Furthermore, in vivo fast‐scan cyclic voltammetry (FSCV) was used to ascertain the impact of ZL006 on morphine‐induced increases in dopamine (DA) efflux in the nucleus accumbens shell (NAc shell) evoked by electrical stimulation of the medial forebrain bundle (MFB). ZL006 attenuated morphine‐induced increases in DA efflux at a dose that did not have intrinsic effects on DA transmission. We also employed multiple intravenous drug self‐administration approaches to examine the impact of ZL006 on the reinforcing effects of morphine. Interestingly, ZL006 did not alter acquisition or maintenance of morphine self‐administration, but reduced lever pressing in a morphine relapse test after forced abstinence. Our results provide behavioural and neurochemical support for the hypothesis that inhibition of PSD95‐nNOS protein–protein interactions decreases morphine reward and relapse‐like behaviour, highlighting a previously unreported application for these novel therapeutics in the treatment of opioid addiction.

Keywords: nitric oxide, nNOS, protein–protein interaction, PSD95, relapse, reward

## Abstract

Disrupting NMDA receptor signaling by PSD95‐nNOS protein–protein interactions inhibitors blocked morphine‐induced CPP, attenuated morphine‐induced increases in DA efflux and reduced morphine relapse.

## INTRODUCTION

Excessive glutamatergic activation of N‐methyl‐d‐aspartate receptors (NMDARs) is implicated in altered forms of neural plasticity in opioid addiction. 1 , 2 Glutamatergic transmission is specifically implicated in forming associative memories, during both the opioid experience and opioid withdrawal. 3 NMDARs and μ‐opioid receptors (MORs) co‐localize in various brain regions and exhibit bidirectional interactions. 4 , 5 The MOR agonist morphine potentiates NMDAR activity by increasing levels of the signalling molecule nitric oxide (NO). 6 Excessive production of NO is involved in several pathological forms of neural plasticity, such as opioid tolerance, dependence, and reward. 1 , 7 , 8 NMDAR antagonists such as MK‐801 attenuate these negative effects of opioids. 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 However, their clinical use is limited by adverse side effects (e.g., learning and memory impairment, motor ataxia, cognitive dissociation, and increased lethality). 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 Neuronal nitric oxide synthase (nNOS) catalytic inhibitors also suppress opioid reward, tolerance, and dependence 1 , 5 , 18 , 19 , 20 but lack of isoform selectivity similarly contributes to unwanted side effects. 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 Thus, indirect mechanisms to disrupt NMDAR signalling without the negative side effects of NMDAR antagonists or non‐selective NOS catalytic inhibitors are needed to leverage the clinical potential on NMDAR‐dependent NO signalling for suppressing opioid addiction.

NO production via the NMDAR‐nNOS signalling cascade is dependent upon the scaffolding protein postsynaptic density 95 kDa (PSD95), which tethers nNOS to NMDARs. 26 , 27 Upon excessive NMDAR activity, nNOS interacts with PSD95 to stimulate NO production. 6 , 28 Inhibitors of PSD95‐nNOS protein–protein interactions attenuate pathophysiological conditions involving excess glutamatergic signalling in animal models of pathological pain, 29 , 30 , 31 ischaemic injury, 32 traumatic brain injury, 33 and post‐traumatic stress disorder. 34 Small molecule inhibitors such as 2‐((1H‐benzo [d] [1,2,3] triazol‐5‐ylamino) methyl)‐4,6‐dichlorophenol (IC87201), the first‐in‐class disruptor of PSD95‐nNOS interactions, inhibit the binding of nNOS to PSD95 in vitro without altering nNOS catalytic activity. 29 A structurally related PSD95‐nNOS inhibitor, 4‐(3,5‐dichloro‐2‐hydroxy‐benzylamino)‐2‐hydroxybenzoic acid (ZL006), reduced infarct size and cerebral ischaemic injury following middle cerebral artery occlusion and reperfusion in wild‐type but not nNOS−/− mice. 32 We previously reported that IC87201 and ZL006 directly inhibited binding of purified PSD95 and nNOS proteins, suppressed NMDA‐stimulated cGMP production (a marker of NO formation), and reduced glutamate‐induced cell death at levels comparable with the NMDAR antagonist MK‐801. 31 We also showed that both IC87201 and ZL006, administered systemically, suppressed inflammatory and neuropathic pain and neurochemical markers of inflammation‐evoked neuronal activation in rats. 30 , 31 Both PSD95‐nNOS inhibitors are blood–brain barrier penetrant and, unlike MK‐801, did not impair motor function, spatial memory, source memory, or basal nociceptive thresholds. 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 , 35 Accordingly, we hypothesized that inhibition of PSD95‐nNOS interactions may disrupt NMDAR‐dependent opioid reward without the unwanted effects of NMDAR antagonists of nNOS catalytic inhibitors.

In the present study, we asked whether small molecule PSD95‐nNOS inhibitors, IC87201 and ZL006, are inherently reinforcing and whether they can effectively block morphine‐induced reward using a conditioned place preference (CPP) paradigm. We used fast‐scan cyclic voltammetry (FSCV) in combination with electrical stimulation of the medial forebrain bundle (MFB) to measure the impact of ZL006, the best characterized PSD95‐nNOS interaction inhibitor to date, on changes in electrically evoked DA efflux in the nucleus accumbens shell (NAc shell) in the presence and absence of morphine. We also evaluated effects of ZL006 on the acquisition and maintenance of morphine self‐administration and on the relapse of morphine seeking after forced abstinence.

## METHODS

### Drugs

IC87201 and ZL006 were synthesized by the laboratory of Ganesh A. Thakur in the Center for Drug Discovery at Northeastern University (by PMK and SG). IC87201 and ZL006 were dissolved in a vehicle containing 20% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) and 80% of ethanol:emulphor:saline in a 1:1:8 ratio and administered i.p. at 10 mg/kg in a final volume of 2 ml/kg injection 30 for CPP and voltammetry experiments. In the self‐administration experiments, ZL006 was dissolved in a vehicle containing 3% of DMSO and 97% of ethanol:emulphor:saline in a 1:1:18 ratio and administered i.p. at 10 mg/kg dose in a final volume of 2 ml/kg injection. The dose selection was based upon our previous studies showing maximal efficacy in inhibiting pain behaviour, 30 without producing motor ataxia, 30 decreasing ambulatory activity, 33 or impairing spatial or source memory. 35 Morphine hydrochloride was obtained from the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA), dissolved in a physiological saline solution and administered at 6 mg/kg i.p. for CPP and FSCV and at 100 μg/kg/infusion for self‐administration. 36

### Subjects

All procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at the Indiana University Bloomington. Male Sprague–Dawley rats (Envigo, IN) were singled‐housed upon arrival and given ad libitum access to water and food and maintained on a 12‐h reversed light/dark cycle. Rats were subjected to at least 48 h of acclimation after arrival before starting any experimental procedure.

### Conditioned place preference (CPP)

We used a three‐chamber CPP apparatus (Med‐Associates Inc., Fairfax, VT, USA), which contained a central neutral chamber with grey walls and two side conditioning chambers with distinct visual cues on the walls: one chamber with black and white vertical stripes and one with black and white horizontal stripes. The floors were made of wire mesh in a grid pattern. The chambers were separated by computer‐controlled guillotine doors that slid upward to allow access to all three chambers. Photobeams detected the location of the animal in all three chambers and were controlled by Med‐PC software (Med‐associates Inc., Fairfax, VT, USA). We used the same protocol described in our previous publications 37 , 38 , 39 (Figure 1A). Briefly, rats were allowed to habituate for 20–30 min in the experimental room prior to placement in the CPP apparatus. All experiments were performed during their dark cycle. On days 1 to 3, rats were placed into the central chamber and allowed to habituate for 5 min. Then, the guillotine doors to the two flanking conditioning chambers automatically opened, and the animals were able to explore all three chambers for 30 min (1800 s). The time that the animals spent in each chamber was recorded. On day 3, an assessment of baseline chamber preference was conducted to confirm that the rats did not demonstrate a bias for any particular chamber prior to pharmacological manipulation (i.e., pre‐test). Rats were excluded from the experiment if they spent less than 360 s (i.e., 20% of time) or more than 1440 s (i.e., 80% of the time) in either conditioning chamber. 37 , 38 , 39 On days 4 to 11, rats received repeated pairings of drug (days 4, 6, 8, and 10) and vehicle (days 5, 7, 9, 11) on alternate days. We evaluated whether IC87201 (10 mg/kg i.p.) and ZL006 (10 mg/kg i.p.), administered to the drug‐paired chamber, would produce reward or aversion when administered alone. Separate groups received morphine (6 mg/kg i.p.) in the drug‐paired chamber or vehicle (i.p.) in both chambers. Finally, we examined the impact on morphine‐induced CPP of IC87201 (10 mg/kg i.p.) and ZL006 (10 mg/kg i.p.) co‐administered with morphine (6 mg/kg i.p.). The total injection volume (2 ml/kg) and number of injections were the same across all groups. Animals were placed into either the left or right chamber immediately after injection to achieve drug (or vehicle) pairings. On day 12, rats were again allowed to explore all three chambers for 30 min, and their chamber preference was evaluated in the drug‐free state (i.e., post‐test).

### Fast‐scan cyclic voltammetry

In vivo anaesthetised FSCV was used to ascertain whether disruption of PSD95‐nNOS protein–protein interactions by ZL006 suppresses morphine‐induced DA efflux in the NAc shell. We measured changes in extracellular DA in the NAc shell evoked by the application of biphasic stimulations into the MFB. 40 , 41 , 42 , 43 Rats were anaesthetised with urethane (1.6 g/kg i.p.) and placed in a stereotaxic frame (David Kopf Instruments, Tujunga, CA, USA) with a heating pad underneath the subject to maintain body temperature throughout experiments. The skull surface was exposed, and 2 mm diameter craniotomies were made in the skull to position the Ag/AgCl reference electrode, a bipolar stimulating electrode, and a carbon‐fibre microelectrode (Figure 2A). The coordinates anteroposterior (AP), mediolateral (ML), and dorsoventral (DV) were referenced to bregma. The stimulating electrode was positioned in the MFB (−4.6 AP, +1.3 ML, −7.5 DV), the carbon‐fibre microelectrode was positioned in the NAc shell (+1.2 AP, +1.4 ML, −6.6 DV), and the reference electrode was placed in the contralateral cortex. Final DV coordinates for the carbon‐fibre microelectrode and the stimulating electrode were based on optimizing the electrically evoked DA signal and were not changed for the duration of the experiment. Carbon‐fibre microelectrodes were fabricated by inserting a single carbon fibre T650 (6.0 μm diameter, Cytec Engineering Materials, West Paterson, NJ, USA) into a borosilicate capillary tube (1.2 mm outer diameter; Sutter Instruments, Novato, CA, USA) and pulling a taper using a vertical micropipette puller (PF‐2 Narishige, Tokyo, Japan). The carbon‐fibre microelectrode was held at a potential of −0.4 V, and every 100 ms the potential was ramped to +1.3 V and back at a rate of 400 V/s. The currents were amplified and recorded using a potentiostat (EI‐400 Cypress systems Lawrence, KS, USA), computer‐controlled interface boards (National Instruments, Austin, TX, USA), and TarHeel CV software (ESA Bioscience, Chelmsford, MA, USA). Electrical stimulation was computer generated and passed through a constant‐current generator (custom‐made). Software‐controlled biphasic stimulation pulses were applied to a twisted bipolar electrode (Plastics One, Roanoke, VA, USA), with tips separated ∼1 mm. Stimulus intensity was 300 μA, with a biphasic pulse duration of 4 ms (2 ms for each phase); trains were applied at a frequency of 60 Hz for 0.4 s (i.e., a total of 24 pulses). Recordings were sampled with at least 5‐min intervals after a stimulating train. To determine changes in the amplitude of electrically evoked DA, signals were recorded under baseline conditions and were analysed to determine the average peak amplitude (i.e., maximal concentration of DA evoked by electrical stimulation [DA]max). Recordings from baseline (i.e., 15 min prior to i.p. injection) and following drug injections were analysed, and values were normalized to the subject's baseline [DA]max. Carbon‐fibre microelectrodes were calibrated after experimental data collection, and currents recorded at peak oxidative potential for DA (~+0.6 V) were converted to DA concentration based on post‐calibration peak currents using DA (1 μM) buffer solution containing (in mM) 12 Tris–HCl, 1.2 CaCl2, 1.25 NaH2PO4, 1.2 MgCl2, 2 Na2SO4. FSCV recordings were statistical analysed, relative to baseline, across the entire 90‐min post‐injection interval from animals receiving injections of vehicle, morphine (6 mg/kg i.p.), ZL006 (10 mg/kg i.p.), or ZL006 (10 mg/kg i.p.) co‐administered with morphine (6 mg/kg i.p.).

### Lever training

Prior to catheter surgery, rats were food restricted (15 g/day) and pre‐trained to lever press for food in operant chambers (Med‐Associates Inc., Fairfax, VT, USA) equipped with two levers (referred to as left and right levers). First, rats were exposed to a single magazine training session (30 min) where a food pellet was delivered every 60 s with both levers retracted. Next, rats were trained (four sessions) to lever press (fixed ratio 1; FR1) for food on the two levers. The session started by inserting one lever and rewarding each of 10 responses on that lever, then retracting the lever, and inserting the other lever and rewarding each of 10 responses on it. The system alternated between levers until 60 food pellets or 60 min elapsed. 36 , 44 Rats were returned to ad libitum food and the catheter surgeries were performed. After surgical recovery, rats were food restricted again and re‐trained (two sessions) to lever press for food. Finally, all groups were returned to and maintained on ad libitum food during the entire self‐administration experiments 36 (Figure 3A).

### Jugular catheter surgery

A backmount catheter was constructed and surgically implanted into the left jugular vein of rats (300–350 g) under isoflurane anaesthesia as described previously. 44 Briefly, a silastic tubing was passed subcutaneously and inserted 3.5 cm into the jugular vein. 45 , 46 Rats were allowed to recover 1 week following catheter implantation before resuming food lever re‐training. Catheters were flushed daily (200 μl) with a heparinized saline solution (100 units/ml) before and after the drug self‐administration sessions.

### Morphine i.v. self‐administration

Animals were tested once daily in 50 min drug self‐administration sessions as described in our previous work. 36 , 44 Operant chambers (Med Associates Inc., Fairfax, VT, USA) were equipped with grid floors, a house light, two retractable levers (referred to as left and right levers) and an infusion pump. Operant chambers used for self‐administration were different and located in another room from those used for the lever training. Levers were randomly assigned as active or inactive for every animal. Each session started with the two levers extended, lever presses on the inactive lever resulted in no infusion while the required number of presses on the active lever resulted in delivery of one infusion paired with a light cue (i.e., discrete cue). Specifically, the infusion pump and light cue turned ON for approximately 6 s, and 6–8 μl were infused based on the rat's body weight. Each infusion was followed by a 5 s timeout period. Levers retracted during an infusion and time out. A morphine concentration of 100 μg/kg/infusion was used for all experiments based upon previous studies in our lab. 36 , 44

In the acquisition experiments, rats were allowed to self‐administer morphine for 10 consecutive days: 5 days on FR1 and 5 days on FR3. This operant schedule training ensured that animals learned to distinguish between the reinforced and non‐reinforced lever. Rats received ZL006 10 mg/kg or vehicle i.p. 30 min before each of the 10 acquisition sessions. The outcomes of once daily injection (i.p.) of ZL006 10 mg/kg or vehicle were examined over the last 5 days of acquisition. The numbers of infusions, and active/inactive lever presses were compared between groups.

In the maintenance experiments, a new group of rats was first allowed to self‐administer morphine for 10 consecutive days as before, 5 days on FR1, and 5 days on FR3. Then, rats continued on FR3 until stable or baseline (pre‐drug) infusion intake was attained. The criterion for stable (i.e., baseline) morphine intake was reached when the rats exhibited less than 20% variance in the number of infusions for three consecutive days. 45 After meeting baseline criteria, the animals received ZL006 (10 mg/kg i.p.) or vehicle (i.p.) 30 min before the self‐administration session for 5 days (i.e., treatment). We analysed the number of infusions, and active/inactive lever presses between groups. Comparisons were also made between baseline and treatment for each experimental group, within‐ and between‐subjects, as appropriate.

In the relapse test, a separate cohort of animals was trained to self‐administer morphine for 10 consecutive days as before: 5 days on FR1 followed by 5 days on FR3. This group then experienced 21 days of forced abstinence (i.e., withdrawal) in their home cages followed by a single cue‐induced drug seeking session (i.e., relapse test). In order to minimize the experimenter‐induced stress on the relapse test day, animals were handled daily during the forced abstinence period. This daily handling was carried out in a different room from where the self‐administration experiments were conducted to avoid previous environmental/context drug‐associations. Rats were treated with ZL006 (10 mg/kg i.p.) or vehicle (i.p.) 30 min before the relapse test session. On the relapse test, subjects were placed back into to the drug self‐administration environment/context (i.e., operant chambers) with an identical configuration; however, active lever pressing resulted in the delivery only of the discrete cue previously paired with morphine, but no morphine was infused. We analysed active/inactive lever presses and made comparisons between the last day of morphine self‐administration (i.e., last day of morphine acquisition) and the relapse test day.

### Statistical analysis

Data were analysed by analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Bonferroni post hoc tests. The Geisser–Greenhouse correction was applied to adjust the lack of sphericity in repeated measures ANOVA. Based upon our prior hypothesis and prior results in CPP and voltammetry studies, differences between groups in a specific direction in the self‐administration experiments (i.e., treatment is effective) were determined using an unpaired Student's t test (one‐tailed). All statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism (GraphPad Software, La Jolla, CA, USA). Data are presented as mean ± SEM, and p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

## RESULTS

### Rats exhibit robust conditioned place preference to morphine

When rats received vehicle in both chambers (i.e., vehicle‐vehicle pairings; Figure 1B), there was no difference in the time spent in each chamber. The interaction between conditioning phase and drug treatment was not significant (F 1,12 = 1.535, p = 0.2390), and no main effects of vehicle treatment (F 1,12 = 0.001873, p = 0.9662) or conditioning phase (F 1,12 = 0.05027, p = 0.8264) were observed. Thus, vehicle–vehicle pairings did not produce either CPP or conditioned place aversion (CPA). By contrast, repeated pairings with morphine (6 mg/kg i.p.) produced robust CPP to the drug‐paired chamber compared with the vehicle‐paired chamber (Figure 1C). A significant main effect of drug treatment (F 1,20 = 5.503, p = 0.0294) was observed, the interaction between conditioning phase and drug treatment was significant (F 1,20 = 7.688, p = 0.0117), but no overall effect of the conditioning phase (F 1,20 = 0.2862, p = 0.5985) was observed. Post hoc comparisons revealed that rats exhibited an increased time in the morphine‐paired versus vehicle‐paired chamber on the CPP test day (p = 0.0017) but no such difference was observed at baseline prior to conditioning, consistent with the development of CPP for morphine.

### PSD95‐nNOS interaction inhibitors alone do not cause reward or aversion

IC87201 (10 mg/kg i.p.) treatment alone did not alter time spent in the drug‐paired versus the vehicle‐paired chamber on the CPP test day (Figure 1D). The interaction between the conditioning phase and drug treatment was not significant (F 1,12 = 0.2044, p = 0.6592), and no main effect of drug treatment (F 1,12 = 2.125, p = 0.1706) or conditioning phase (F 1,12 = 3.946, p = 0.0703) were observed. Similarly, in a separate group of rats, ZL006 (10 mg/kg i.p.) treatment alone did not alter time spent in the drug‐paired chamber versus the vehicle‐paired chamber on the CPP test day (Figure 1E). The interaction between the conditioning phase and drug treatment was not significant (F 1,18 = 0.0008305, p = 0.9773), and no main effect of drug treatment (F 1,18 = 0.5107, p = 0.4840) or conditioning phase (F 1,18 = 0.04688, p = 0.8310) was observed. Thus, PSD95‐nNOS inhibitors did not themselves produce reward or aversion.

### PSD95‐nNOS interaction inhibitors block morphine‐induced CPP

Combination treatment with morphine (6 mg/kg i.p.) + IC87201 (10 mg/kg i.p.) blocked morphine‐induced CPP (Figure 1F). The interaction between the conditioning phase and drug treatment was not significant for the morphine + IC87201 combination treatment (F 1,14 = 0.8627, p = 0.3687), and no main effect of drug treatment (F 1,14 = 0.147, p = 0.7072) or conditioning phase (F 1,14 = 0.5245, p = 0.4809) was observed. Similarly, in a separate group of rats, combination treatment with morphine (6 mg/kg i.p.) + ZL006 (10 mg/kg i.p.) blocked morphine‐induced CPP (Figure 1G). The interaction between the conditioning phase and drug treatment was not significant for the morphine + ZL006 combination treatment (F 1,18 = 1.059, p = 0.3170), and no main effect of drug treatment (F 1,18 = 0.003592, p = 0.9529) or conditioning phase (F 1,18 = 0.123, p = 0.7299) was observed. Thus, two structurally distinct PSD95‐nNOS inhibitors blocked morphine‐induced CPP.

### ZL006 blocks morphine‐induced increases in DA efflux in NAc shell evoked by electrical stimulation of the MFB

Morphine increased the extracellular [DA]max signal relative to the baseline DA signal at 15 (p = 0.0014), 30 (p < 0.0001), and 45 (p = 0.0457) min post‐injection (Figure 2B). To ascertain whether disruption of PSD95‐nNOS interaction has any effect on morphine‐induced increases in DA efflux, we characterized the effects of ZL006 on [DA]max. The extracellular [DA]max signal subsequently declined from 60–90 min post injection compared with the maximal levels observed 15–30 min post‐injection (p < 0.05 at each 60–90 min post‐injection time point, respectively) (Figure 2B). ZL006 alone (10 mg/kg i.p.) did not alter the extracellular [DA]max signal relative to vehicle at any time point (p > 0.9999; Figure 2B). Neither vehicle, ZL006, nor ZL006 + morphine altered the extracellular [DA]max signal relative to baseline at any post‐injection time point (p > 0.9999; Figure 2B). Pharmacological manipulations altered [DA]max in a time‐dependent manner (interaction: F21,119 = 2.587, p = 0.0007; Figure 2B). [DA]max did not differ between groups overall and trended to decrease across the recording interval irrespective of drug treatment (Drug: F 3,17 = 3.067, p = 0.0561; Time: F 7,119 = 2.477, p = 0.0249). Post hoc comparisons revealed that morphine increased evoked [DA]max at 15–30 min post‐injection relative to all other groups (p < 0.05 at each time point; Figure 2B). Notably, co‐administration of ZL006 (10 mg/kg i.p.) with morphine (6 mg/kg i.p.) prevented the morphine‐induced increase in evoked [DA]max at 15 (p = 0.0041), 30 (p < 0.0001), and 45 (p = 0.0245) min post‐injection (Figure 2B). Representative voltammetry scans of electrically evoked DA signal (Figure 2C left panels) and colour plots (Figure 2C right panels) illustrate that the DA signal measured pre‐drug and after the co‐administration of ZL006 + morphine remained essentially unaltered.

### ZL006 did not alter the acquisition of morphine self‐administration

ZL006 (10 mg/kg i.p.) did not change the outcomes of the acquisition of morphine self‐administration (Figure 3). Rats in this experiment received i.p. injections of ZL006 or vehicle during the 10 days of morphine self‐administration that comprise the acquisition phase: 5 days in FR1 and 5 days in FR3 (Figure 3A). The interaction between treatments and FR was not significant for number of infusions (F 1,9 = 1.57, p = 0.2417), active lever presses (F 1,9 = 0.05735, p = 0.8161), or inactive lever presses (F 1,9 = 0.466, p = 0.5120). Interestingly, we detected an initial descending trend (i.e., first five sessions, FR1) in the animals receiving ZL006 in the infusion number (FR1, VEH vs. ZL006, t (9) = 2.031, p = 0.364, unpaired t test, one‐tailed; Figure 3B) and active lever presses (FR1, VEH vs. ZL006, t (9) = 2.031, p = 0.364, unpaired t test, one‐tailed; Figure 3C). However, these differences disappeared when reaching the end of the acquisition phase (i.e., last five sessions, FR3) (Figure 3B,C). No differences were found in the inactive lever presses at any time in the acquisition phase (Figure 3D). Furthermore, no interaction effect was found in the overall acquisition between sessions and treatment in the infusion number (F 9,81 = 1.972, p = 0.0532; Figure S1A), active lever presses (F 9,81 = 0.8499, p = 0.5729; Figure S1B), or inactive lever presses (F F9,81 = 1.108, p = 0.3668; Figure S1C).

### ZL006 did not alter morphine intake during the maintenance phase of morphine self‐administration

ZL006 (10 mg/kg i.p.) did not alter morphine intake during the maintenance phase of morphine self‐administration (Figure 4). Animals in this experiment completed the acquisition phase of morphine self‐administration without receiving any (i.p.) drug treatment and continued self‐administering morphine daily until a stable behaviour was reached (baseline), after which rats were injected with ZL006 or vehicle for the following five consecutive morphine self‐administration sessions (Figure 4A). No interaction was found between drug treatment with ZL006 or vehicle and infusion intake (F 1,8 = 1.138, p = 0.3172, Figure 4B), active lever presses (F 1,8 = 0.4351, p = 0.5280, Figure 4C), or inactive lever presses (F 1,8 = 0.0004363, p = 0.9838, Figure 4D). Furthermore, no differences in infusion intake across sessions were found for the vehicle group (F 1.5,6.2 = 0.4503, p = 0.6109, Figure S2A) or the ZL006 group (F 2.58,10.32 = 1.591, p = 0.2511, Figure S2B). In addition, no interaction was found between the sessions and lever presses in the vehicle group (F 7, 28 = 0.702, p = 0.6701, Figure S2C) or ZL006 group (F 7,28 = 1.64, p = 0.1653, Figure S2D), and the differences between active and inactive lever presses remained similar and significantly different (p < 0.001) in both groups during the baseline and treatment.
